title: EXPENSE RATIO: 6 THINGS TO KNOW
series_label: WHAT IS AN EXPENSE RATIO AND HOW DOES IT EAT RETURNS: 6 THINGS TO KNOW

concepts.title: The Definition
concepts.body: An expense ratio is the annual fee a fund charges, expressed as a % of your investment. 0.50% means the fund keeps $5 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. It's deducted automatically from fund assets — you never write a check, but you always pay it.

visual_spec.callout_text: Annual fee, % of assets. 0.50% = $5/yr per $1,000 invested. Deducted automatically. You never see a bill — but you always pay it.

concepts.title: What's Inside The Fee
concepts.body: The expense ratio bundles management, administration, marketing (12b-1), and sometimes custodial costs. Index funds are cheaper because they don't pay a team to pick stocks — they just hold the index. The result: VOO at 0.03% vs the average active equity fund at 0.60%+.

concepts.title: Good Vs Bad Ranges
concepts.body: Rough guide for 2026: 0.03%–0.12% is good for equity index funds (VOO 0.03%, FXAIX 0.015%, VTTSX 0.08%). 0.20%–0.40% is mid-range (some active ETFs). 0.50%+ is expensive (most traditional active mutual funds). Bond and specialty funds can run higher.

concepts.title: The 30-Year Hit
concepts.body: On $100,000 held for 30 years at a 7% gross return, the difference between 0.04% and 0.65% in expense ratio is roughly $187,000 less in your final balance. The fee compounds against you, just like returns compound for you — only in reverse.

concepts.title: Gross Vs Net Return
concepts.body: Gross return is what the fund's holdings did. Net return is what lands in your account. The expense ratio is the bridge: a 7% gross fund with a 0.50% expense ratio delivers 6.50% net. The smaller the bridge, the more growth stays in your pocket.

visual_spec.callout_text: Gross return − expense ratio = net return. A 0.50% fee on 7% gross = 6.50% net. That 0.50% gap compounds for decades.

concepts.title: How To Check Yours
concepts.body: Every fund's expense ratio is on its fact sheet, prospectus, and your brokerage's fund page. Look it up before you buy. Search '[ticker] expense ratio' to find the official figure fast. If the only index-fund alternative is below 0.20%, paying more for an active version is a hard case to make.

sources_footer: Sourced from Vanguard VOO/VTI fact sheets, Fidelity FXAIX prospectus, FINRA Fund Analyzer, SEC investor.gov
